summary: The note traces the history of Arkansas Post, the first European settlement in Arkansas, founded by Henri De Tonti in 1686. It describes the post's role as a fur-trade center, its relations with the Quapaw and Chickasaw peoples, and its economic struggles. It also covers the repeated relocations of the post in 1749, 1756 and 1779, tied to conflicts such as the Seven Years' War.
one_line: Overview of Arkansas Post, Arkansas's first European settlement, founded in 1686 and moved several times during the 1700s.
key_facts: The first European settlement in Arkansas was Arkansas Post, established in 1686 by Henri De Tonti.
Arkansas Post disbanded for unknown reasons in 1699 and was reestablished in 1721 in the same location.
Arkansas Post was located slightly upriver from the confluence of the Arkansas River and Mississippi River.
The remote Arkansas Post was a center of trade and a home base for fur trappers in the region.
French settlers at Arkansas Post mingled and in some cases intermarried with Quapaw natives, sharing a dislike of the English and Chickasaw, who were allies at the time.
A moratorium on furs imposed by Canada severely affected the post's economy, and many settlers began to move out of the Mississippi River Valley.
Scottish banker John Law tried to entice settlers to emigrate from Germany to start an agricultural settlement at Arkansas Post.
John Law's efforts failed when the Mississippi Bubble he created burst in 1720.
The French maintained the post throughout this period mostly due to its strategic significance along the Mississippi River.
The post was moved back further from the Mississippi River in 1749 after the English, with their Chickasaw allies, attacked.
The post was moved downriver in 1756 to be closer to a Quapaw defensive line and to serve as a trading post during the Seven Years' War.
The 1756 move also aimed to prevent attacks from the Spanish along the Mississippi.
After the Seven Years' War ended, the post was moved upriver out of the floodplain in 1779.
